deep.reconstruction:
The page is undated; context in the bundle suggests the late 1830s. The main content (upper right and upper left) is the spherical mean-value theorem for the Newtonian potential, the core of Art. 20 of Gauss's 'Allgemeine Lehrsätze in Beziehung auf die im verkehrten Verhältnisse des Quadrats der Entfernung wirkenden Anziehungs- und Abstossungskräfte' (1840).

(1) Setting. A sphere has radius R and centre O, with surface element ds. V = ∫ dm/r is the potential of a mass distribution, where r is the distance from the mass element dm to the surface point. M is the total mass inside the sphere. A = ∫ dm/ρ is the potential at the centre due to the masses outside the sphere, where ρ is the distance of dm from O.

(2) Claim (upper right). ∫ V ds = 4π R² A + 4π R M. Gauss first wrote a different right-hand side, something like 4π(RR/?)A + 4πM/R. He struck it out and replaced it with the corrected line. The corrected line has the right dimensions: area × potential gives R²·(mass/length).

(3) Derivation (upper left column):
- ∫(dm/r)·ds = ∫ dm ∫ ds/r, by interchanging the order of integration.
- Lemma (my explicit statement): for a unit point mass at distance ρ from O, ∫_sphere ds/r = 4πR²/ρ if ρ > R, and = 4πR if ρ < R.
- Proof of the lemma (my filling): with ds = 2πR² sinθ dθ and r² = R² + ρ² − 2Rρ cosθ, we have r dr = Rρ sinθ dθ. Hence ∫ ds/r = (2πR/ρ)∫ dr = (2πR/ρ)[(R+ρ) − |R−ρ|].
- For exterior masses this gives ∫ 4πRR·dm/ρ = 4πR² ∫dm/ρ = 4πR²·A (the lines '∫4πRR.dm/ρ' and '∫dm/ρ').
- For interior masses each dm contributes 4πR·dm, giving 4πR·M.
- Equivalently, the mean of V over the sphere is A + M/R. In particular, if no mass lies inside, the mean of V over the sphere equals V(O) (Gauss's mean-value theorem).

(4) Sketches.
- Circles with a small body inside and a point or radius drawn are sphere-and-mass configurations for (3).
- A nested-shell drawing is labelled V = a, V = A (and possibly V = r). These are likely the companion propositions of 1840: if V is constant on a closed surface or sphere enclosing no mass, then V is constant (= a) throughout the interior. Applying ∫V ds to such a configuration forces V to equal its boundary value. This reading is plausible but not certain.
- A lone '∫V ds' repeats the central integral.

(5) Isolated formula: y = e^(−1/x²). This is the classic C^∞ function all of whose derivatives vanish at x = 0, so its Maclaurin series is identically 0. No context is given. It may be a reminder that knowing a function locally, or all its derivatives at a point, does not determine it. That would be relevant to uniqueness questions for potentials, but this connection is conjecture.

(6) Arithmetic (lower left), mostly identifiable:
- 5798 − 4692 = 1106, and ×10 gives 11060.
- 11060 − 9173 = 1887.
- 2·9173 = 18346.
- Other figures (24013/24813, 524, 6535, 148, 206, 13) have unclear relations.
- Weights: '8500 gr / mgr', '23' (with marginal 14 and 11), '10800 mgr 1''' and '10,800 Kupfer'. These look like weights in milligrams of copper (wire or bar) per unit length (1 inch?). They probably belong to Gauss–Weber magnetic or galvanic apparatus (multiplier coils). A small square-with-circle and a hatched rectangle (coil cross-section?) accompany them.

(7) Rotated German text (right): 'Mein … / Unter allen den schönen Sachen / U[nd] … / Frommen'. This appears to be a non-mathematical verse or letter fragment.
errors: The first version of the right-hand side, roughly 4π(RR/?)A + 4πM/R, is wrong: the interior-mass term must be 4πR·M, not 4πM/R. Gauss struck it out himself and corrected it to 4πRRA + 4πRM.

No errors remain in the corrected formula. The interchange of integration order is unproblematic for a distribution with no mass on the sphere itself. Mass lying exactly on the sphere is not treated on the page.
The lemma ∫ds/r = 4πR²/ρ resp. 4πR is used without written proof, which is standard.

results.what: Integral of the Newtonian potential over a sphere: ∫V ds = 4πR²A + 4πRM (A = potential at the centre from exterior masses, M = interior mass). Equivalently, the spherical mean of V equals A + M/R.
results.modern_name: Gauss's mean value theorem for harmonic functions/potentials (spherical mean value property)

results.what: Surface integral of 1/r over a sphere: 4πR²/ρ for an exterior point, 4πR for an interior point

results.usually_credited_to: Cauchy, Résumé des leçons sur le calcul infinitésimal (1823)

results.modern_name: Constancy of a potential inside a mass-free region bounded by an equipotential surface (maximum-principle-type uniqueness)

deep.surprise_reason: The main content is a working draft of Gauss's own published mean-value theorem (1840), so it is routine and well known as his. The only mildly notable item is that he jotted Cauchy's flat function e^(−1/x²) next to it, possibly in connection with uniqueness or analyticity of potentials. That function was published by Cauchy in 1823, and the page has no context showing Gauss used it in any original way.

checkable.asserts: For an exterior point (ρ=3 > R=1), ∫ds/r over the sphere = 4πR²/ρ = 4π/3
For an interior point (ρ=1 < R=3), ∫ds/r over the sphere = 4πR = 12π
The mean value of V over the sphere equals A + M/R

The marginal subtractions and doubling are correct

transcription_corrections: Line 1: the struck-out part reads roughly 4π(RR/?)A + 4πM/R (with crossings). Only '= 4πRRA + 4πRM' stands as the valid result.
Left column, last line: '∫dm/ρ' rather than '∫dx/ρ'.

'V = r' (left sketch) is uncertain. It is written inside the small closed curve near a drawn circle and may be 'V = a' or 'V = r'. The other labels read 'V = a', 'V = A' (twice; the second may be a different stroke variant).
'24013' may be '24813'; the second digit is blotted.
'14 8500 gr mgr' likely means 8500 with annotations 'gr' (Gran?) and 'mgr' (milligram) above it. The 14 and 11 are separate marginal numbers to the left.
'10800 mgr 1''': the superscript above 10800 looks like 'mgr' and the 1'' denotes one inch. The line below reads '10,800 Kupfer'.
The rotated German text is better read as 'Mein … / Unter allen den schönen Sachen / U[nd] / [struck word] / Frommen'. It is non-mathematical.
